utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Belinda Pidwell, Crispian Smith, Roseanna Morton and Tom Hannis for the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Ms. Lacey, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present. He already signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we begin this morning's work, there are two matters that the Chamber would raise. One is, lest I forget to do it at 10.20 for certain procedural reasons -- well, there are certain procedural matters with which we have to deal, and therefore the first break will be 30 minutes, not 20 minutes. The second matter is that yesterday there was filed a motion for the testimony of a witness to be heard via videolink and because that witness is scheduled to begin -- to testify on the 1st of December, we would respectfully respect expedited responses from the Defence by today week.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have -- I announced that I have a brief matter before we start. But, first, I would like to say that we do not oppose the motion for videolink. We understand the reasons for -- for that. And I believe I'm talking on behalf of both -- both Defences, and we will not oppose that, therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The second thing is, Your Honours, you are aware that we filed yesterday the notice of adjudicated facts. However, as you are aware, we are still talking about the exhumation issue, and it's -- it's a pretty complicated because of the sheer volume of the data that is -- that has been provided to the Defence. We believe that, if we could have a day off, perhaps the week after the week of the 15th, we would -- it will help us to resolve some of the matters with our friends from the Prosecution in respect of these exhumations. There is possibly also some talks about some addition stipulations, but this is in the -- in the pipeline. Now, Your Honours, I talked with my friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, for that week, the 15th, they have one witness who is -- who is scheduled to come on Wednesday for two days, Wednesday and Thursday. And they don't have any more witnesses -- basically they have but they are flexible about it. So what we were -- what we would like to propose is that we get that Friday off so we can discuss -- which is, I believe, the 19th of November, so we can discuss these issues concerning the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Actually, in terms of the question of a non-sitting day there were a number of dates kicked around internally, and the 19th is one of those days, so everything may fall into place, in that respect, Mr. Zecevic. But we would ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Where we were, and again, I'm speaking internally, is that we were looking at the 17th, would the 19th in fact be more convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it is entirely up to -- to the Trial Chamber. We can have it either the 17th or the 19th. So whatever is -- whatever is the preference of the Trial Chamber, if I may say so. We will -- we will abide by that, but all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We have had discussions before court on this issue, and the -- it would be preferable if we could take the non-sitting day on the Friday. The only reason I say that is that the witness is confirmed to come on the Wednesday. I'm not sure how long his testimony is going to be or the cross-examination, in light of the fact that the cross-examination estimates are usually an overestimate. And accordingly, from the witness's perspective, if he could start on the Wednesday, finish on the Thursday, and then from whatever time he finishes we could finish for the week. From a scheduling perspective that would be better rather than have him run over the weekend. But, Your Honours, we're in your hands. I can amend his travel dates if Your Honours prefer to sit on the other day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, speaking about the witness Ms. Pidwell mentioned, we give our initial assessment at the outset, but I don't believe that I will need more than an hour or an hour and a quarter for the cross-examination. So I think that we can deal with him in one day. I'm not sure how much time the OTP think they will need, but the cross-examination by the Defence probably will not last longer than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, it now looks very much like Friday, but we would confirm that in the course of today, we hope. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So if there are no other housekeeping matters, we would need to lower the blinds in order to have the witness escorted in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there is one other matter that I intended to -- something that Mr. Zecevic said that I meant to have clarification on. The -- when you talk about stipulation, in terms of the -- sorry, not stipulation, exhumations, did I understand to you say that both sides are still talking about this? The reason why I asked for clarification there is that you would recall that just before the site visit, we had reached the point where the written motions and responses having been in, counsel on both sides had responded to invitation to expand on this orally, and we have actually been looking at that material. So I do correctly infer that we could -- as it were, suspend our work on this, pending a further joint report from counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, you're putting me in a -- in a pretty awkward position. Let me -- let me explain what is -- what is the essence of our talks. Your Honours, before you there is one -- there is one legal matter, one legal question. Whether the -- the -- the Prosecutor is allowed to add additional victims which are not in the schedules. Is that the -- that is the question and we're not talking about that. That is a question which we made our submissions to the Trial Chamber and we expect the Trial Chamber to rule on that. Now, what we are talking is a step further. I requested -- or, actually, the Defence has requested all the underlying material concerning the exhumations, and we are concentrating only on the victims that are in the schedules. At the moment, of course, because that's our position. Now, we are now trying to find out the solution if we can agree to a number of -- of these victims from the -- from the exhumation reports for the number of victims which are now in the schedules to the indictment. And that is the task that we are undertaking at this point. I hope have I been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. So we will continue our analysis and we will wait to hear from counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks. Could the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. I need to point out to you that the solemn declaration that you just made does expose you to the penalty of perjury, should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, are we in closed session? This witness has full protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're in open session now. Sir, just please be aware if I ask you any questions not to name any members of your family or other people who could identify you. Do you recall being called up for active duty in May or June 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I was called up around 2.00 a.m., and I responded. There's a pharmacy and a court building, and behind them there was the rally point. I waited until 6.00 a.m. I was the only one to report there, but when nobody else came, the duty officer entered my name on the list and then I went to the factory. But afterward, nobody called me again. We were supposed to go to Banja Luka to get weapons, but I didn't go with them. I went to work, and I wasn't called again. On the same day another unit went to Banja Luka, and weapons were brought to the stadium there and it was distributed to the TO. But they were all Serbs. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you were the only one who turned up, do you know why that was?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I don't know why. But I know that I was responded to call-ups even for exercises and I was always on time. There was a courier to alert me. I dressed in my uniform and arrived there around 2.00, but there was no one. Around 6.00, in front of the fire-fighters building, there were some people, but they were all Serbs. I don't know why nobody else came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that these weapons were brought to the stadium and distributed to the TO. Were you given a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: No. I wasn't called again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now some questions about the events which took place in Kotor Varos on the 11th of June, 1992. Firstly, can you please explain the significance of the date of the 11th of June. It's a special day, and can you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim, and that day was a religious holiday called Kurban-Bajram. We go to the mosque to pray. We have two holidays, the other is Ramadan-Bajram, then we go to the mosque too. And I went to the mosque on that day, because only there can the religious ceremony be held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what time you went to the mosque on this morning?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Around a quarter to 5.00. But at 5.00 I was in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without saying any names, did you go alone, or did somebody else accompany you?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I went up to the mosque alone, on foot, from my home to the mosque. It's -- the distance is about 800 metres to 1 kilometre, maybe. I walked alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in the mosque with you that morning?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: About two dozen. I didn't count. But thereabouts, not more than that. It was not prayer time yet. The time for Bajram prior had not yet come, only the Sabah prayer had begun. But we didn't -- or, rather, I wasn't even able to finish the Sabah prayer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Then -- may I state the name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Muhamed Sadikovic arrived with weapons. He was wearing a blue camouflage uniform. That was a police uniform. He was a police officer. He entered the mosque with weapons and said, The police has been taken by the Serbs. Whoever wants to join the fight can go with me over the river, and who doesn't want to can go home. And I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Mr. Sadikovic arrived with these weapons and -- and made this announcement, did that come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes. Because the situation was so tense that it could be expected at any moment. However, I didn't expect it on that day. A curfew was imposed and there were guards on the streets, but I didn't expect it to happen on Bajram day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to show you now a photo, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 3419.81, please. It's tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I'm well-informed by my assistants, the last four photographs are not on the 65 ter list. I'm referring to tabs 8, 9, 10, and 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall at the beginning of the trial, we submitted a high tech compilation of photographs. When we started with the municipality of Kotor Varos, we had some maps which then zoomed in onto different locations in the municipality, and that was tendered under 65 ter 3419. And there's a whole lot of subpoints in that. These photos are part of that. The photo disclosure covers a whole lot of other photos we have various different angles of the same shots, but they're all on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, please just be careful with your answers, but do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to make some markings on the photograph. And there's a pen there that you can use. Now, firstly, with the number 1, could you mark the Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the number 2, could you mark, please, the administration building of the Pilana, the sawmill?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: That is here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there's a restaurant section to that administration building. Are you able to mark that with the number 3?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You can't see it, because the corner is here and there's a new building that was constructed, so one cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you have marked with the number 2 is the restaurant portion where it should be; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes. Because it's the same building, only administration is on the first floor, and on the ground floor is the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we now go into private session, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, when you said "gate," which gate were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: It was the Proleter hide factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see it on the photograph there?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: It was right here, on this street. This street leads directly to the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the first occasion that you'd seen soldiers outside of that gate?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Let me note that while I was leaving to go to the mosque, nobody was there. So when I left to go to the mosque. When I was on my way back some of them were there. As from the gate of the sawmill and below the gate, they were five or six of them going. The street was full. They were also armed and going towards them. And I tried to move to my brother's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... and as you tried to divert, did they intervene in any way?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: As soon as I tried to divert and made a few steps they said, Stop, all three of them, and, Come here. Because we had nothing, arms or anything, so we had to retrace our steps and go back to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you went back to them, what did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: There were two others with them who used to work at the leather processing factory, one from Vagani and another one from Kotor Varos. I do not know that names, and I didn't know any of the others. They searched all three of us. They frisked us to see if we had any weapons. When they saw that we didn't carry any weapons, they took us to a room down there which had already been prepared for prisoners. It was empty except for the straw mats that were on the floor and the three of us were the first who were brought in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were brought into a room, sir, where was that? What factory or building did that belong to?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: That was with within the Proleter complex. To the right was the administrative building and straight was what used to be the mechanic work-shop and then it was changed. The new building was built and empty remained there. They also had some sort of a depot. It was all part of the Proleter complex.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in that room with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, it is not really clear to me what the Proleter complex is, the same way I was struggling with the witness's testimony about the gate he was talking about. He also mentioned Proleter complex. Can we eventually show that on the map and tell us what that is? It's a leather factory, so it's not a sawmill?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'll clarify that Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring back to the photograph, do we see the Proleter factory complex here on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we please redact lines 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist if we make some more markings on this photograph. Can you -- do you see the gate of the Proleter factory on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Could I do it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've marked it with a red circle. And can you indicate --

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- exactly what this factory was? Can you tell us what this factory was?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: It was a complex of six factories. There was an electrical plant, there was the Bosna Shoe Factory, the Mladost shoe factory, Galko, Boksvel, and also a clothing factory. So that was the complex called Proleter. And the sawmill is a separate one, up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'll tender that image now, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P16 -- sorry Your Honours. As Exhibit P1686.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were taken into this factory complex, which particular factory were you taken into?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Proleter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the -- in this building?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Hardly ten minutes. Then they called out just my name, so I went out. We called them the specialists. The camp mates call them the specialists. Those who wore green camouflage uniforms and green -- or, rather, Red Berets and the policemen had the other ones, though they used to swap uniforms, and it would depend whichever somebody had -- this they wore. He called out my name, he put handcuffs on my hands, and took me to the administrative building of the Proleter factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: He took me in. He made me lean against the wall turned to him. He hit my mouth with his rifle. He split my lip. He also asked me whether I had any money. I said I didn't. Then he hit me another two or three times and then, though I was all bloody, he took me outside. He also knocked out one of my teeth on this occasion. When I went outside, he took me to the gate, and up at the gate, was already one man. Can I say his name?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Dzevdo Turan. He also handcuffed and he was standing up there, and the two of us were taken together to the sawmill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, if I may interrupt briefly. I don't know if you intend to return to it, but just in the event that we lose it later, the witness referred to there practice of swapping uniforms. I'm curious to hear more about that. If it is something with which you intend to deal, I'm content to wait until you come back to it. If not, perhaps we can deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Witness, you referred to the Red Berets on the policemen. They used to swap uniforms. Could you tell us some more about that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just mention Dule Vujicic, who was an active-duty police officer. He had a blue camouflage uniform and a blue cap. When he would go to mopping up operations and when he was returning, he would come with a green camouflage uniform and a green cap. Is that enough or should I say more? This is just one example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you tell us the colour cap again, please. You said he came back with a green uniform and a green cap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A red cap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I am wondering is whether -- how widespread this pattern was from your observation, if you're able to assist with that. How common was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These days it was raining practically every day. And if people got wet - was that intentional or not - if they had some sort of uniforms, they would put them on. I cannot say what the reasons were, but I can just say that I did see them in different uniforms. I know that they changed them. Was it according to their needs or was it the same to them, that's something I don't know. But the same people would wear both kinds of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we carry on with -- with what happened to you, do you know what happened to the two boys who initially accompanied you from the mosque?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Could we redact the line -- sorry page 22, line 6, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now please describe what happened when you came to the Pilana sawmill.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Dzevdo and I were brought into a room there. Where it was in the restaurant, there were between 15 and 20 people there, including women - the wife of our president, Ante, was there - they were sitting in it corner. This so-called command, I don't know what they were, but you had to address them, and Dzevdo and me were brought in front of them and they wanted to take off our handcuffs and said that they were not guilty, but they were looking for the keys and couldn't find them. So they took us both outside and in front of the gate of the sawmill towards the main road, I was standing there with handcuffed hands, and Dzevdo was beaten in front of me. I had a feeling that it was like squeezing a sponge, that was how they hit him, so when you would let the sponge, then it would extend and this was how he started to swell. Then they came along to me and one of them hit me and I became unconscious. When I came to, they told us to board a jeep and that they would move us to the SUP, but that not a single drop of blood should fall anywhere inside the jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned this so-called command. How many people were there in positions of authority at the Pilana sawmill on this day?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: When I say the command, there was just a desk there and a few of them sitting there, but I didn't dare to look them in the face. I just hung my head. Whenever they said anything, they would hit with you a baton or a rifle or anything. So I was just standing like that and they were shouting. It was not a command. I'm not sure how to call them at the moment, because anything like that never existed before. In the corner of this building, the men who brought us there addressed them and then when they took us outside they ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Green camouflage ones with red berets. There was not a single one there wearing a blue uniform at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone -- any of them as being local people from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- did anyone accompany you in the jeep?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Dzevdo and myself sat at the back, and in front there were four of them with rifles - the driver and three others - and we were at the back. The jeep was kind of opened at the back. You lowered this thing down and we were sitting there, and that was how we arrived to the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the jeep was a military or a police vehicle? Or -- if you don't know, just please say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Not at the moment. I couldn't be sure and say for certain. I know that ... that the jeep --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his answer. Something about the jeep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreter missed the last part of your answer. You said something about the jeep.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: It was higher. It wasn't a simple car, but what was the colour or what was the make, this is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until this point in time, had anyone told you why you had been handcuffed and detained in this manner?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Nobody said anything. No one said a thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of the people who were -- who you saw at the sawmill, what was their ethnicity, the ones who were being detained, not the -- not the soldiers or the police?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Only Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we carry on, sir, I just want you to look at another photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: It's P38. It's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the gate and the restaurant and the administrative building of the sawmill as seen from the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described being beaten outside the sawmill, can we see from this picture where that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Here, at the gate. Should I draw it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please mark with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall where the jeep was parked?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please mark with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other vehicles there; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see anything at the moment. I know that I was brought to the gate when they were beating us, and the jeep was parked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If I could tender that at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1687, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I now have another photograph, it's P50. It's tab 4. Sorry, my apologies, I'm wanting tab 5, P49.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes. It's the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the police station in the jeep, what happened as you -- as you got out of the jeep?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Here, in front of the police station, there was a line of reserve guys, both in olive-drab uniforms and in blue camouflage uniform. We were taken out of the vehicles and they led us to the building, and those that were standing in line beat us. And when we entered the building, to the right, there was a room, and that's where they threw us in. We had already been badly beaten. And there was some 15 or 16 people in there already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people do you estimate were standing outside the police building in uniforms at this time?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Twenty to 30, at least. I was in no position to count them though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the men who accompanied you from the sawmill to the police station, were they the same ones who had initially brought you to the sawmill, or were they different people?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: The one that had brought us from the sawmill, they told us, You're going inside. And as we started walking, nobody ever asked us anything. They simply started beating us. I don't know what they had been ordered to do. But that's how it turned out anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And am I correct to infer different guards brought you from Pilana to the SJB building?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: We were taken from the leather processing plant to the sawmill. There were five or six. And then people brought us from the sawmill to the police station. I didn't look at their faces, so I can't say whether they were the same guys or others. But they were wearing the same kind of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to confirm, what uniforms were they?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Green camouflage uniforms with red berets. And the man who hit me in the leather processing plant wore the same kind of uniform. I later found out that he was from Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you left the jeep and walked to the -- into the SJB building, and you've described the crowd of people who were there, were there any other people like you, people who were being detained there at the time, to your knowledge, or were you not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: When I was taken out of the jeep, my hands were still tied and his too. We were both beaten. And when we reached the entrance of the building they said they would throw us in, and then they untied us both. They removed our cuffs and simply pushed us inside, as I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing any other vehicles outside the police station at this time?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: There were two APCs. I saw them in front of me. They told us, Come out. And we did, and the people were already standing there. The APCs were blue. They were police APCs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you mark on the photograph, please, where in the building the room was that you were initially taken into. Please mark it with a letter A.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Here, through the door, and then to the right. A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you entered that room, were you able to see what was happening down the corridor in the other areas of the entrance way?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I was there for eight days. The hallway was full all the time. People were leaning against the wall with three fingers, and it -- people were coming and going all the time. I couldn't really look at their faces to see who was who. But there was constant screaming and beating. And then -- but they threw me in that small room in which there were only Croats and Muslims who I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see police officers in regular police uniform present during your -- this time?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: In that room which you enter when you come in, I know there was police officer from Travnik. He was a bit overweight. But nobody wore a regular police uniform. They were all wearing camouflage blue. And I don't know if I saw anybody else while they were taking me there. There wasn't really time to look around much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any police officers that you personally knew there during your detention?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Later on, yes. Dule, Vujicic. Sejdo was a police officer, too. I saw him. There was one guy just across the road. What's his name? I can't remember his name now. He is also a police officer. He has a house. I saw about half a dozen of them at that moment while I was there. We were in the police building for seven or eight days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those seven or eight days, were you processed in any way? Were you -- did you have to fill in some forms and provide your personal details to the people who were detaining you?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Somebody came to call somebody's name approximately once in two hours. But during these eight days, we were lost in time. We didn't know whether it was day or night. The window was closed with boards, so it was dark inside all the time. Zdravko Samardzija was one of those who interrogated people, and those who were interrogated by him were released. I was taken from the small room to another room. There was my brother and other neighbours, all of them Croats and Muslims, and we stayed there for seven or eight days. Whoever was taken to be interviewed by Zdravko Samardzija was released, but not us. We weren't taken there. We were taken to the building behind the pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at that photograph again, sir, can you - using the police building as a reference point - please describe where the building was behind the pharmacy?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Well, if you set off from the police toward Doboj there's the corner storage, then there's a building, then the pharmacy, and the court building. There was a road between them, and then there was the TO warehouse with the weapons. They had cleaned it out. And they took us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we go on to that in more detail, I want to ask you some questions about what happened during the seven or eight days while you were in the police building. How did you -- how were you fed?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: We got maybe a slice of bread or some fish or a -- or some canned food once a day. Nobody really asked questions about that. As long as they didn't beat us, but they did beat us regularly. Somebody called Dinko's name, I later on heard from the camp inmates that he was from Laktasi or thereabout, I taken to the room near the -- near the gate, near the entrance, and one of them asked me about my family, beat me with his pistol, he kneeled down on me and he asked where was my family, and I said, At home. He said -- he asked me who else have I got, and I said, My brother is in the other room and my father, he is in the country. But then he told the guard, Let him stand there. I'll bring his brother. And he did, and he beat him too. And he asked me where I was. I said, At the mosque. What you did you do there? I said, I went to pray, and then he started, What do you need to pray for? And started cursing and swearing. And then he said he would go and check whether I had spoken the truth, whether I was really in the mosque or at the front line, but he didn't come back and he didn't beat me anymore. Then the guard was told to call Samardzija. Samardzija --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last two or three sentences. He is going rather fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreter couldn't quite keep up with you. Could you please repeat the last three sentences. Just -- we have from ... you said that he was asking you whether you were really in the mosque: "Or at the front line, but he didn't come back and he didn't beat me anymore. "Then the guard was told to call Samardzija." And then could you please carry on from what -- from there.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: The guy didn't go to fetch Samardzija, and when that one returned he continued to beat us. We were both beaten for about an hour and a half. And then he ordered us -- or, rather, he took us to that room to stay there and that he would check, and unless we were speaking the truth he would come and kill us. But he -- he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What uniform was this guard wearing?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: He was wearing a blue camouflage uniform, a police officer. He's from Kotor Varos. I don't know his real name. I know roughly where he lives. About -- his house is about 100 metres from the police station, toward Banja Luka, right by the Serbian church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Pidwell, if this is a convenient point, we'll take the break now. Yes, so the witness could be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we return in 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, the Chamber has a few decisions to communicate to the parties. First of all, as for the day in which we would not sit, the week after the coming, the Chamber has decided to declare Friday, the 19th of November, a dies non, so as to allow the parties to complete the negotiations on the stipulation and, notably, the death certificate database. Next thing is a response to -- or a decision on two Prosecution motions, of which the Chamber has been seized on 15th and 21st of October, requesting the Chamber to admit the evidence of Witness ST-221, pursuant to Rule 92 ter and to grant the Prosecution leave to examine him for 30 minutes. And, secondly, seeking leave to reinstate on its 65 ter exhibit list a photograph of ekonomija farm, Rule 65 ter 2289; and also to add two maps of the Zvornik which are the 65 ter 3680 and 3681; and a video footage of the ekonomija farm and the Gero slaughter-house which is Rule 65 ter 3682; and, finally a photograph of the old town area of Prijedor which is Rule 65 ter 3683. Neither Defence team has responded to these motions. As to the first amendments of the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, the Chamber is satisfied that the proposed items are prima facie relevant and have probative value. As visual aids, they will assist the Trial Chamber in its deliberations and the Chamber considers the nature of these items, the Defence have been on sufficient notice and that no prejudice is suffered by the Defence by adding these item to the 65 ter exhibit list. Accordingly, we grant the Prosecution leave to add the Rule 65 ter numbers 2289, 3680, 3681, 3682, and 3683 to the 65 ter exhibit list. Turning then to the other request to admit the evidence of Witness ST-221, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, the Trial Chamber finds that the requirements of this rule are met and that it is in the interests of justice and in the interests of judicial economy to hear his evidence purpose to this rule. Nevertheless, the Trial Chamber will only consider the actual admission into evidence of Witness 221's statements at the conclusion of his testimony which is the normal practice that we have applied in this trial. Furthermore, the Chamber is persuaded that, in particular, because of the video footage that the Prosecution seeks to show him, an additional ten minutes are added to the 20 minutes set forth in the Trial Chamber's guide-lines on admissibility and presentation of evidence, so we grant the Prosecution altogether 30 minutes to take this witness through his statement. Finally, the Prosecution has also filed a motion regarding the time set aside to examine Witness ST-222 in-chief, and if I'm not mistaken, the Prosecution has asked for altogether two and a half hours to have this witness examined in-chief. Witness ST-222 is going to be called viva voce, and the Chamber has considered the matter and has decided that the Prosecution can have one hour to take Witness ST-222 through his examination-in-chief as viva voce. But, Mr. Hannis, when that hour has been used, it looks as if the Prosecution is very close to having exhausted the time it was given for completion of its case. We are working to find out exactly how much time there is left, and we will have this figure ready by Monday, but this is a clear indication from the Chamber to the Prosecution that, in the Chamber's view, the Prosecution is, indeed, very close to having exhausted the time that it has been given. So we will revert to this matter on Monday. And I hereby give the floor back to Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Firstly, can I seek to tender the photograph that was previously on the screen and marked by the witness. That wasn't done previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1688, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to ask you a follow-up question from something you said before the break. You mentioned that during your time in detention in the police station in this room, somebody called names out every two hours. Can you tell us who that somebody was?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: They just called people -- the names of people that came to their minds. There was no system in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person who came to call the names out, was that person in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the uniform of that person, or those -- the variety -- the people who came to call the names out?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we please redact the last sentence please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we're still in open session so if would you please be careful with names. You've spoken a little bit about there man called Samardzija. Do you know who he was, or what his position was?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: We only know that all that he and Sejdo Tatar communicated with the people in all surrounding villages telling them that there was a truth -- truce, that they shouldn't shoot and they visited those villages. When we were in the police station, we felt safer and didn't think that anybody would beat us because he was their superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten during your time in the police station?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Hardly an hour or two could elapse without somebody coming in and beating you or taking you to the hallway and beating you there. So it went on non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go into closed session for this next section, please. Closed and private.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Private session, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We're back in open session, sir, so just be careful with names with this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this period of seven or eight days that you were detained at the SJB building in Kotor Varos, were you taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: During the eight days I was there, and then later on, they took me to the prison there behind the court-house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were taken to the prison?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: No one was telling anyone anything. They would just take you with guards. There were about 15 or 20 of them and eight of us. We had small containers for food, and on foot we went all together to the prison, and they accommodated us in room number 3. And there were six rooms in total.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If can I ask you to look at a photograph, please. It's tab 9, 65 ter 3419.79. If can you take a moment, please, sir, to look at this photograph. Are you able to identify some of the buildings on there; and, in particular, are you able to identify the municipal prison in Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Here is the prison. Should I mark all that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mark with the letter A the prison.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you mark the court-house with the letter B?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us how far the prison was from the SJB building and in which direction you walked?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: From the police building. The police building is down there, and it's about 700 or 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, the arrow pointing to the left in the photograph is what the witness was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If that could be admitted and marked, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said, sir, that you were taken by about 15 or 20 guards by foot to the prison. Do you recall what uniform the guards were wearing when they accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: They were coloured uniforms, both the blue camouflage uniforms, and the green camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- how long did you stay in the prison there?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: The 11th ... almost five or six months. I don't know exactly. On the 13th of November, I was transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who was in charge of the prison when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: It was one Zaric but I don't know his first name. I know that his nickname was Djiba. He was an active-duty police officer. There was also Aleksa Vucenovic and Ljubo Arsenic and there was also one Tesic, from Ripiste, who used to work in the sawmill. The four of them were guards for three, three and a half or four months, until they were relieved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a name by the name of Slobodan Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I know Slobodan Dubocanin. He was escorted by one man called Kubura and another man. I used to see them. They visited us on three occasions. Once it was maybe three and a half months after we had arrived to the prison. They had beaten us every day, every night, until Slobodan told them one evening that nobody would be beat us anymore, and after that, no one beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you understand his authority to be in the prison? You said he came and told hem to stop beating you and they did. What was his position in relation to the prison, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Well, they were talking about some mopping up and something but we didn't know much about that in the prison. It was wartime already and I had been taken in on the very first morning. But, in any case, I know that he was from the special unit, the special forces, this is how they called themselves. In the camp they would just say specials and we would try to run and hide because we knew that they would beat us and he was whether the commander or what, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Just -- I confirm that the Stanisic stipulates to 521, 523 and 525. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you saw Slobodan Dubocanin at the prison, what uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: A green camouflage uniform and a red beret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was an occasion when the Red Cross came to the municipal prison in Kotor Varos in early October. Can you please tell us about that visit and the events of that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how we arrived to this line of questioning and why this is relevant in terms of the adjudicated facts, and which specific adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The adjudicated fact is Adjudicated Fact 1201 which stated that the Kotor Varos elementary school and the municipal prison were run by the Serb special police. That is the fact that was denied. The witness will give evidence about a visit to the prison by people in authority, including one of the accused, and in my submission that is directly relevant to his relationship with the prison and authority over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but if this witness is about to talk about the activities and the conduct of the accused, then it is outside the bounds of this testimony. We were not notified that this witness would talk about this, and I believe the decision of the Trial Chamber is that when we deal with adjudicated facts that these witnesses can only talk about these adjudicated facts and this is why they were called, rather than to introduce in this way testimony about the activities and conduct of the accused, because the Defence has not been notified that this would be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is in the proofing note. And it is also in his statement, although portions of it are. The issue -- the issue is: Who was in charge of the Kotor Varos prison? That's the issue which the Trial Chamber considered and denied -- considered in denying this previously adjudicated fact. It's the Prosecution's position that the prison was run by the police, special police, who, we say, were under the command of the accused. So the fact that I'm leading evidence that the accused was present at a prison is directly relevant to who had authority over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, the witness replied who was responsible. He responded to that. So what is the point? The question was clear: Who was the commander and who were the guards? And the witness answered that question. So where does the special police fit in? And where does this adjudicated -- or, rather, offered fact arise? The witness was clearly asked, Your Honours: Who was the prisoner warden? Who was in charge of the prison, and what the position of other persons? So what else is there to ask? Not in one of his previous statements did this witness mention the accused. It was only yesterday that in the proofing note, we received notification from the OTP that he has changed his testimony now. So had we been aware of this fact, we would have included that in the cross-examination of some of the witnesses whom we have examined about this earlier. If the Trial Chamber allows this is line of examination, then I will request that some of the witnesses who have been cross-examined be re-called here so that I could cross-examine them once again about this adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There is always the question, the next question, these adjudicated facts in terms of context, but I'm concerned, Ms. Pidwell, about Mr. Krgovic's complaint that this particular point was new to them and only became apparent when they saw the proofing note of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I'm going to have to ask the witness to take off his head phones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... thank you. Yes. Yes, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours in the witness's -- this witness has not testified before. In his statement that he gave to the OTP in 2000, he named a variety of people during the course of his statement. He spoke about a delegation coming to the Kotor Varos prison on this day, and he named certain people who were present. Now, in his statement the refreshes he makes is to Slobodan Zupljanin. Now, we know there is a man who existed by that name. Throughout his -- his statement, he interposes first names and last names. For example, there's a reference to Dubocanin in his statement. And he puts the wrong first name. He puts Samardzija first name with that person and interposes them throughout. Now in proofing, I asked him some questions about this delegation who came to the Kotor Varos prison and he told me that it was Stojan Zupljanin who attended on that day because his brother had told him that. That is as much as he is going to say. That is the evidence that came out of proofing and that is what is in the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But if this clarification, for want of a better word, only became apparent yesterday, and bearing in mind the explanation that you have given, and reminding myself and, with respect, you, that counsel can't give evidence. It's the witness who -- who -- who gives the evidence, the -- aren't we left with the position that, for the first time, yesterday, it was apparent -- I was going to use the word "clear ," but from what you said isn't clear, but was apparent that it was the second accused of whom the witness spoke. And, therefore, the -- Mr. Krgovic's claim about being caught by surprise is valid. And if I may add, if this is a new dimension to the Prosecution's case, then he, as he said, it's something which not having had the opportunity to address with relevant witnesses before, he would have to -- may have to go so far as to make an application to have those witnesses re-called. With all of that, is it a matter that you would wish to press, Ms. Pidwell?

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Firstly, Your Honour, the proofing note was sent on the 2nd of November; it wasn't yesterday. Secondly, there is a risk when we call these witnesses viva voce that new evidence will come out at a late stage. We only meet with them a couple of days before, and once we know that there's something new, it goes out in a proofing note at the earliest opportunity. The issue is: Who ran the Kotor Varos prison? When he was asked about that, this is the information he gave us to, and, in my submission, it is wholly relevant to the issues before the Trial Chamber, and Mr. Krgovic can deal with it in cross-examination, but that's about as far as I can I take it. If Your Honours want to hear the evidence, the witness is here, and he can be cross-examined on it right now. I'm not aware that any other witness has given this evidence before, so I'm not sure which witnesses Mr. Krgovic is referring to when he says he wants them re-called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It appears to the Trial Chamber that it is unavoidable that this evidence, from the witness who is presently on the stand, could be led. And we're not unmindful of the concerns Mr. Krgovic has expressed. But, of course, we -- it is something that he would deal with in cross-examination and we will see where we go from there. We are alerted to the possibilities of this, but the evidence which the OTP wishes to lead at this point is clearly relevant and, as I said, we see no reason why we could or should seek to prevent her from leading it. More than that, we wouldn't say at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll go back to my question, which was there was a -- a day in early October that the Red Cross came and visited the municipal prison in Kotor Varos. Can you please tell us your recollection of that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted) Zdravko Pejic. There was Slobodan Zupljanin, and five or six to the extent that we could see. I didn't know everybody so well. I knew Slobodan well. He worked in the factory. He [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] was a director there. Whereas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat this part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, the interpreter has asked if you could repeat the last part of your answer. We have: "I knew Slobodan well. He worked in a factory. I was a director there." And then if could you continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of why these people were at the prison on this day?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Since the Red Cross came on the first day, where they had come from and how, I really don't know. But we knew that we would all be registered. That was probably -- that information was probably forwarded because the guards, the active-duty police officers were only there to let us go to see the toilets, and so on. But when there were people in green camouflage uniforms with red berets, they couldn't prevent them from doing anything until Slobodan Dubocanin banned them from entering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think you slightly misunderstood my question, sir, and I wasn't clear and I apologise. What was your understanding of why these other people were there this day? You mentioned Djekanovic, Slobodan Zupljanin, Stojan Zupljanin and a couple of others. Why were they present at the prison on this day?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I simply understood that their intention was to prevent our registration. Some people were taken to the basement of the court for that purpose. We had been there for months. One man --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter again didn't catch all of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last sentence, sir, "One man ..."

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Now I'm not sure what exactly I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. Did you personally see this delegation of people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am aware that there has been a couple of names are slipping out, but I believe the Court Officer has caught them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time for the regular break now, and that would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the record, we reconvene for the final session under Rule 15 bis; Judge Delvoie being absent. And I paused after saying final session, because I understand that -- from the Court Officer that the Prosecution has a concern about completing this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's just really a reserve position. I inquired of the Court Officer of the possibility to have an extended session to ensure that we complete the witness today. I have been assured by my learned friends that it is likely that we will finish within this session. But the extension maybe is a reserve position just in case he runs over for a few minutes thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the Court Officer will make the necessary inquiries and we'll see where we go. Before we continue, the matter with which we sought to deal earlier about the new evidence coming -- the new -- new evidence coming from this witness, the -- to the extent that either side may have a concern as to whether the ruling that we made allowing the Prosecution to lead this evidence qualifies or contravenes the extant rulings on 92 bis and the Rules, generally. That is not the position. This, as we see, is a situation determined in its own circumstances arising from the fact that there appeared to us to be relevant evidence which only came to the attention of the Prosecution just before the witness was about to lead his evidence. And I repeat what I said earlier, that there are procedural remedies which may have to be applied by the Chamber to remedy any disadvantage which counsel for the Accused Zupljanin would have experienced as a result of this. And, in any event, to state the obvious, the Trial Chamber would have to determine the relevance and weight of -- of this evidence in -- at the end of the exercise. So I trust that both sides are -- have a clear understanding as to where we are with this evidence, which was -- which only came about because of the gateway, as it were, of the context of the adjudicated fact in question and in respect of which the Prosecution was permitted to lead this evidence. Yes, Ms. Pidwell, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before the break, you were telling us about a day when a group of people came to the Kotor Varos prison, and, on this day the Red Cross were there. Do you recall how long this group of people stayed at the prison for, on this day?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: They stayed only for about two or three minutes in our room. They took him out to the office where the guards were and they stayed at least two hours in that office. And then the man from the Red Cross returned and continued registering us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "they took him out," are you referring to the man who had come from the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you, in fact, registered by the Red Cross on that day?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time at the municipal prison in Kotor Varos, did the guards change at any time, or did they remain the same?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: There was this group headed by Djiba for at least four and a half months. And then three Croats escaped from the pig farm where we had to go to work. And then they were replaced and another group arrived in their stead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other group that arrived, do you know if they were police officers or what their positions were?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Zdravko Rutic, he was commander then, otherwise he worked at the Proleter leather processing company. Then there was Radenko Keverovic. There was Dule Vujicic, but he didn't see us often, he was an active-duty police officer. There was Kretic, who was an active-duty police officer from Skender. And then there was a guy from Vagan whose name I don't know. Then there was also Radenko Djukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I want now to ask you to watch a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And if I can have, please, P1579. It's tab 7 in Sanction. I'm not going to ask the interpreters to interpret what is going on. I'm going to ask the witness to identify people on the video and make some comments so I don't think we need any commentary or the sound to be played. If we could play it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: And pause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This first portion is very dark. Do you see -- you see the men standing there. Are you able to comment on --

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on -- or do you recognise any of them or what they're wearing?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I don't recognise them. But the uniform is a green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this room?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I think that I was taken to this room once to be interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry. For the record, that was 5:49.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: The quality gets a little better now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can just look at this person in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Sorry, it was -- we've skipped it. That's all right. We'll just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I know his face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think you know his face?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Because, on one occasion, I asked the guard to take me home. I had some gold. And he sat me in a car and drove me home. We took the gold and we were on our way back. And somewhere by the sawmill, or between the sawmill and the church he caught up with him and he sat in the front and I was sitting in the rear. And then when he asked the guard whether anybody had talked to the prisoners and he said no. When I -- he -- he left the car in front of the pharmacy because he had to go elsewhere and when we drove on he told me, This is their boss. But I don't know his name. I was driven by Aleksa Vucenovic who told me so then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this, what you just said, was that during your detention in the SJB building or in the Kotor Varos prison?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: The prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's an APC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us where -- where that is?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: It's in front of the police station. And that building is the university.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Just play it a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If can you comment on what you're seeing in front of us, sir, if you can.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: This was a daily occurrence. Whoever entered here had to lean against the wall with three fingers and then we would be beaten. But this man, we can't see him being beaten. People were naked from the waist up and badly beaten up and bloody. There was blood all over the floor in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: We're just going fast-forward to 13:38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this house?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes. It's right next to the hospital. It's a Muslim house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I know his nickname but not his name. They called him Tarzan, and he used to work in the textile factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Can we go to 17:30 please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that man?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was guarding me at the police station. He was Djaja from Laktasi.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can go to 19:15, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this house?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes, that's in Vrbanjci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who lived there?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Nisko Kovacevic, Ramo's son. He used to sell leather goods. This is by his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: He was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: If we can go to 22:20, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this gentleman?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: That's Dzevdo Turan, who was taken together with me from the gate of the leather processing factory to the sawmill, and then from the sawmill to the police building. Dzevdo was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on whether this footage was taken -- or when this footage was taken of him, what date?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: He was first brought there to the police, together with me, and as they were in the little room when they called out his name he was taken to Banja Luka and he was also questioned there and then released from Banja Luka. He returned through the woods on foot to his home, and then they imprisoned him again in his home and brought him to the prison behind the court, next to the pharmacy. I'm not sure if this was at that moment. I don't think so. Because, at the time, he was all, as you can see, he is all black and blue. Look at his eyes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I appreciate that was a little disjointed, Your Honour, but in order to expedite the process, I just wanted to show you certain clips of that. That is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have no further questions for you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we have the date of this video or approximate date, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Another witness will come and -- who was featured on the video and will give it the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pidwell. In order to expedite the cross-examination of this witness, Mr. Aleksic will lead, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Before I begin asking you questions, I wish to tell you that personally I really regret what you have gone through and what you have suffered, both you and your family. But as my learned friend and the Judges ask you questions, this is our job. We are professionals and I do have certain questions for you. You gave your first statement to the investigators of this Court on the 12th of August, 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You have a wait a little bit, especially as we speak the same language and because of protective measures as well. Please make a pause and then answer my questions. The interpreter who was present at the time interpreted the statement to you. You said that to your knowledge and recollection, it was true and accurate, and you signed it; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And then, on the 29th of May, 2001, you met, again, with the representatives of the OTP and the Registry of this Court, in order to sign formally a declaration as a witness in accordance to Rule 92. And on that occasion, before signing the declaration, you were again given the opportunity read the statement in your language, and you said that you wished to make some corrections and changes to the statement. Did it happen that way?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I do have copies of these statements here for you, if you want it review them. But, believe me, what I will read is correct. I just want to remind you. As for the changes on the 29th of May, 2001, you introduced five very specific and minute, very detailed changes. Number one, on page 3, paragraph 7 of your original statement, in the statement whiskey, light-haired sergeant, you corrected the word "whiskey" into the word "a tallish man" because in B/C/S it is "viski" and "visoki," and it was an obvious error so you wanted it corrected; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The next correction was that in a sentence words -- something in the sentence of should be left out of the sentence when in the sentence when said something in the sense of [as interpreted], I'll kill them and so on, you said that this part of the sentence should be deleted; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have copies of these statements here together with the changes for the witness, so if he could perhaps have a look at that. Maybe the usher could provide him with the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I will find you where the changes are, just to facilitate matters for you. Please have a look at this. Are these the changes that you wished to introduce at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us not go through these five minute changes. After that, you signed the witness declaration, and you said that the first statement with the additions, which included the changes, was true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge and recollection; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, sir, on the 18th of August this year, you were interviewed as a witness before the federal organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in connection with the same events that you talked about today; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they were federal or state organs, but they came from Sarajevo, from SIPA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Maybe this is my mistake. You know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: When you gave this statement, you were cautioned about your rights and obligations from the Law on Criminal Procedure; namely, that you have to speak the truth because you might be held accountable to perjury then that you were entitled not to answer a certain question if you or a close relative would be incriminated by that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-241
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And after that, you said that you had understood all the legal cautions. And then you began giving your statement, something that I noticed, which is under tab 4, if necessary.
